Liability

/lye-uh-BIL-ih-tee/ · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Liability means a person or thing that counts against you or puts you at a disadvantage; in law, it also means legal responsibility for harm or debt.

The firm's crash-prone accounting software became a liability that cost it two major clients.

Worked Example

Grayline Couriers prided itself on speed, but its twenty-year-old delivery trucks told another story. Breakdowns stranded drivers on the highway, and missed deliveries piled up every week. Repair bills soon cost more than new vehicles would have. The board finally admitted the aging fleet had become a liability and approved its full replacement.

The old trucks are a liability because they create constant risk and expense that put the company at a disadvantage.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

burden: A burden is something difficult or costly to carry — a load of duty, debt, or care that weighs on whoever bears it. A liability is a step more pointed: it is the person or thing that counts against you, weakening your position or exposing you to loss. A burden wears you down; a liability works against you.

drawback: A drawback is a disadvantage or weakness in something that is otherwise worth having — every plan and product has a few. A liability is more serious: it actively counts against you, creating real risk, cost, or legal exposure. You accept a drawback and move on; a liability is what you replace, insure, or cut loose.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

asset: a useful or valuable person or thing

advantage: a condition that puts one in a better position

Where it sits · how directly it threatens real harm — flaw → liability → hazard

flaw vs. liability: A flaw is a small imperfection, while a liability actively puts a person or organization at a disadvantage.

hazard vs. liability: A liability creates risk and cost over time, while a hazard poses a direct, immediate danger of harm.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — liabil

Root — liabil: from Latin ligare via Old French lier, to tie or bind

Suffix — -ity

Suffix — -ity: state or quality of

Put it together

Put it together: From Latin ligare, meaning to tie or bind, which reached English through Old French lier. Someone liable is literally bound to answer for something, and a liability is what binds you to risk or responsibility.

Use the root in a new word: oblige

Use the root in a new word: oblige: Signing the contract will oblige, that is, legally bind, the company to finish the project on time.
